name: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu
role: Bengali saint who spread congregational chanting of Krishna's names
summary: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was a 15th and 16th century Bengali saint who spread devotion to Krishna through joyful group singing. Gaudiya Vaishnavas, including ISKCON, honour him as the founder of their tradition.
about: Chaitanya was born in Nabadwip, Bengal, on 18 February 1486, according to most accounts, and was first called Vishvambhara and then Nimai. As a young scholar he taught Sanskrit grammar and logic. After a trip to Gaya around 1508 or 1509 he is said to have been deeply changed, and he began leading kirtan, group singing of Krishna's names. In 1510 he took monastic vows at Katwa and was named Sri Krishna Chaitanya. He then lived mostly in Puri, visited south India for about two years, and gathered disciples including the brothers Rupa and Sanatana. Gaudiya Vaishnavas believe he is Krishna come in the form of Radha's devotion. He left only eight verses, the Shikshashtakam, yet his followers produced a vast literature. Accounts of his death differ.
kidSummary: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was a Bengali scholar who became a saint and filled the streets with joyful singing of Krishna's names. People say he sang, danced and welcomed everyone. His followers still celebrate his birthday, Gaura Purnima, with songs and special food.

story.title: Nimai of Nabadwip
story.text: He was born in Nabadwip in 1486 and nicknamed Nimai. He was clever and quick, and he started his own school at sixteen.

story.title: A change at Gaya
story.text: Around 1508 he travelled to Gaya for his father's funeral rites. There he met a holy teacher, Ishvara Puri, and his life turned toward devotion.

story.title: Singing in the streets
story.text: Back in Bengal, with friends such as Nityananda and Advaita Acharya, he led large groups in kirtan. A local ruler once banned the singing, but Chaitanya led a large peaceful procession.

story.title: A monk in Puri
story.text: At 24 he took monastic vows and went to Puri. At the Rath Yatra, King Prataparudra swept the road before the chariots, and Chaitanya swept and washed the Gundicha temple.

story.title: A tradition grows
story.text: He spent his last years in a quiet room in Puri. His followers wrote his story and built a faith that still sings his message.

teaches: Chant and sing God's names together

facts.text: Chaitanya was born on 18 February 1486 in Nabadwip, according to most accounts, on a full moon evening during a lunar eclipse, say his hagiographers.
He was named Vishvambhara at birth, called Nimai, and later Gaura or Gauranga for his fair complexion. The name Nimai is linked to a neem tree he was said to be born under.
Stories say baby Nimai stopped crying only when neighbours chanted God's names, and that two thieves who kidnapped him for his jewellery ended up carrying him home.

A childhood legend says Nimai was found playing with a venomous snake in the yard. In another tale he sat on a heap of discarded cooking pots to teach his mother that nothing is impure when used in God's service.
In another legend, a visiting Brahmin cooked an offering for his deity and the child ate it, three times. The Brahmin then had a vision that the child himself was the deity he was worshipping.
A legend says he threw his own brilliant logic commentary into the Ganga so that it would not outshine the work of his friend Raghunatha Siromani.
When a local ruler banned group chanting, Chaitanya led a large peaceful march to the ruler's house. The ruler is said to have supported his cause afterward.
A teaching recorded by Dinesh Chandra Sen says that once you say you love God, all human beings become your brethren, with no Brahmin and no Sudra. He put devotion above caste labels.
King Pratapa Rudra, who wanted to meet Chaitanya, won a meeting after sweeping the road before the Rath Yatra chariot as an act of humble service.
He left only eight verses of his own, the Shikshashtakam, but his movement inspired a large body of writing, much of it in Bengali.
Accounts of his death differ. One work says he died naturally, another says he vanished into the image of Jagannath, so we cannot be sure.
The Hare Krishna mantra, also called the Maha-mantra or 'Great Mantra', has 16 words and 32 syllables and is built from three names: Hare, Krishna and Rama. Chaitanya's movement made it famous.
In 1969 George Harrison produced the Hare Krishna Mantra single by the Radha Krishna Temple. It reached number 12 in the UK, and the devotees appeared on Top of the Pops.

His chant later crossed the ocean. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada began the first recorded public chanting of the mantra outside India under an elm in New York's Tompkins Square Park, now called the Hare Krishna Tree.
The Rath Yatra page links the English word 'juggernaut' to Western impressions of the giant chariot procession of Jagannath at Puri, where Chaitanya spent his later years.
On Gaura Purnima, his birthday, ISKCON temples bathe his image in fruit juices and flowers and offer Chhappan Bhog, 56 kinds of food, then share it as blessed food.
In 1514, on his way to Vrindavan, Chaitanya met two brothers at Ramakeli who were ministers of Sultan Husain Shah. He took them as disciples and renamed them Rupa and Sanatana.
Each year before the Rath Yatra, Chaitanya is said to have swept and washed the Gundicha temple himself with pitchers of water. He began a tradition his followers still keep.
At Gaya, the teacher Ishvara Puri gave him a ten-syllable mantra. Back in Nabadwip he closed his school and gave himself to group chanting, often falling into deep trances.
At 24 he became a monk, partly so that people who saw him only as a local scholar would stop opposing his message. His monastic name became Sri Krishna Chaitanya.
His life was told in Bengali by several biographers, including the Chaitanya Bhagavata of Vrindavana Dasa (about 1535 to 1550) and the three-part Chaitanya Charitamrita of Krishnadasa Kaviraja.
